Step 2: Assemble the robot and compose the scene for pick and place Step 3: Test the controls and run pick-and-place Build your next simulation with SimReady Assets This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm , Robotiq 2F-140 gripper , and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls. For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central , an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog . What makes a robot asset SimReady? SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels: Profile: a group of features for a use case, such as a robot body. Features: capabilities needed for the use case, such as joints that can be controlled. Requirements: checks on the settings needed for each feature, such as a joint’s drive settings. For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can. What comes with the asset, and what do you add? The UR17G , Robotiq 2F-140 , and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper. Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task. What should you check before running a pick-and-place task? A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim. Joint settings: Review the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings. Movement: Test a small arm movement and open and close the gripper. Contact: Confirm that the can rests on the work surface without falling through it. During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below. Build a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content. We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task. Required Software: Install Isaac Sim 6.2, the version used for this example, and check its system requirements. Set up an agent of your choice that can use the Isaac Sim skills. Follow the Agent Skills documentation to make the bundled skills available to your agent. Install the Hugging Face CLI only if you choose the command-line asset download option. Use the USD Search endpoint . Step 1: Download the robot arm, gripper, and beverage can assets Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files. Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ. ~/ASSETS/hf/src/simready-assets-c7fa7615/Robotiq_2F_140/simready_usd/Robotiq_2F_140.usda Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example. Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI. What does asset validation tell you? The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks , which inspect joint-drive settings. SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene. Step 2: Assemble the robot and compose the scene for pick and place With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation. Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python: ./isaac-sim.sh -- enable isaacsim.code_editor.python_server If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below. Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation. You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us: Sample prompt used in this example: Assemble the robot arm <local path to Simready ur17g robot usd> with the gripper <local path to downloded simready Robotiq_2F_140 gripper usd> using the Robot Assembly tutorial in Isaac Sim https://docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/6.2.0/robot_setup/assemble_robots.html. Validate the assembly on completion. The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow. Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim. With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step. Step 3: Test the controls and run pick-and-place Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial . Sample prompt used in this example: Run pick and place with the assembled robot and soda can <path to soda can USD from SimReady library> in Isaac Sim. Ensure you do a contact based grasp for picking up the can and validate the accuracy/placement error for the pick and place as well. Skills used : ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’ The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below. Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed. If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results. Simulation assumptions: Fixed setup: The can starts at a known position, with an anchored robot and clear, flat workspace. No vision was used and collision checks were limited. Simplified can: Deformation and liquid motion are not modeled, so this example does not test crushing. Scripted grasp and motion: A horizontal grasp uses a 2 N·m drive-effort cap chosen through simulation tests, not calibrated to fingertip forces or recommended by the manufacturer. Contact and friction hold the beverage can as the arm follows fixed waypoints without replanning. For hardware gripping-force specifications, see the Robotiq product sheet . These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
body_text: Enterprise Article Published November 13, 2026 Upvote 8 +2 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai :last-child]:mb-0"> Building XYBench Evaluating how an answer helps What the experiments show What this means for evaluation 📄 Paper | 🤗 Data | 💻 Code Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench , a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026. A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem : a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed. Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses. The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal. People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask. Building XYBench We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context. For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem. Evaluating how an answer helps A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem. A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response: Pragmatic solution —records whether a model’s response includes solutions to the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X), checking each separately. Pragmatic emphasis —measures whether a model’s answer focuses on the stated request (Y), focuses on the intended request (X), or balances the two. Misconception identification —measures whether a model’s response steers the user toward the underlying goal (X) while discouraging or avoiding the mistaken approach (Y). In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis. To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis. What the experiments show We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics. Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions. A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal. We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request. A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss. What this means for evaluation Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others. Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction. We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption. title: Put Gemini to work for you
body_text: The best assistant knows you and helps you get things done. Today, you can now hand off even more tasks to Gemini and move on with your day. We’ve built it for anyone who has tasks piling up during all the classes, meetings, and school drop-offs that fill the day. Our goal is for Gemini to save you time and money. Starting now, this update is rolling out free of charge for hundreds of millions of people across the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India, using our new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. We’re also rolling out a set of advanced features, starting in the U.S. How it’s changing my daily routine If your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards are already in the Google ecosystem, Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because this sensitive data already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere. Here’s how I’m using it. Recently, our minivan’s check-engine light came on. Ugh. I pulled out Gemini and told it, "Our minivan is overdue for a service appointment. Please call the two nearest dealerships and figure out how to get an appointment early Friday morning over the next month or so." Because Gemini already knows we drive a 2019 Honda Odyssey and where we live through Personal Intelligence , it found the nearest shops on Google Maps and called both at once 1 . I gave Gemini permission to access our utility portal with the new Google Password Manager integration and asked for it to analyze our past billing statements in my email. Gemini worked for a few minutes, and then nailed it. The primary culprit was our heat pump, which it turns out was kicking on around 4 p.m., right in the middle of peak pricing. My wife and I never would have caught that digging through the PDFs and emails ourselves. I use it for smaller stuff, too. Published November 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 89 +83 Célina Hanouti celinah Follow Victor Mustar victor Follow Bertrand Chevrier kramp Follow Lucain Pouget Wauplin Follow Pierric Cistac pierric Follow Eliott Coyac coyotte508 Follow Julien Chaumond julien-c Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> Run them with the tools you already use How open-weight models are used Routing powered by OpenRouter Pricing Image, video and audio generation See where your requests go Breaking change: custom provider keys What's next Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request. Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same. Run them with the tools you already use The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent: Setup guides for Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Pi and Hermes Agent The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets , compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints . PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference. How open-weight models are used On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ( OpenRouter, October 2026 ). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ). Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models. The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it. Routing powered by OpenRouter OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic. OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing : instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability. When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%. Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id: zai-org/GLM-5.3 # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest # highest throughput zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest # lowest price zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita # only Novita Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide ). Pricing Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details. Image, video and audio generation Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs . See where your requests go On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them: Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to: In your settings , you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization. Breaking change: custom provider keys Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id ( model:provider ) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working. What's next This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next: Connect your OpenRouter account to Hugging Face. More tasks routed through OpenRouter. Try a model , or read the Inference Providers docs to get started. title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run
body_text: Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request. Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same. Run them with the tools you already use The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent: Setup guides for Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Pi and Hermes Agent The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets , compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints . PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference. How open-weight models are used On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ( OpenRouter, October 2026 ). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ). Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models. The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it. Routing powered by OpenRouter OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic. OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing : instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability. When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%. Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id: zai-org/GLM-5.3 # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest # highest throughput zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest # lowest price zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita # only Novita Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide ). Pricing Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details. Image, video and audio generation Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs . See where your requests go On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them: Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to: In your settings , you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization. Breaking change: custom provider keys Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id ( model:provider ) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working. What's next This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next: Connect your OpenRouter account to Hugging Face. More tasks routed through OpenRouter. Try a model , or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.
